newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX to list new generation NYH gasoline contract.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX to list new generation NYH gasoline contract.

text.p: The New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) said Friday it will list a new generation of New York Harbor (NYH) gasoline futures contracts starting on February 12 that will reflect stricter air quality standards.

NYMEX said it will list the so called "complex model" contracts, reflecting the U.S. Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990, for January through March 1998, but did not say when it will extend the listing of the new contracts for additional months.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) will allow gasoline deliverable under the new contract to reflect both the simple model of production or complex model of production for the first three months of listing.

The Exchange later told Reuters it has yet to decide the date when it will list additional complex model contracts, saying there remained a number of key issues NYMEX was still discussing regarding phasing in the new specifications.

Under the current simple model of production, refiners must use specified ingredients to conform to EPA standards, whereas the new complex model will allow refiners greater flexibiltity in using their own formula for reformulated gasoline as long as it burns as cleanly as the law requires.

In terms of cleanliness, the new fuel is a step forward in terms of nitrous oxide (NOx) emissions, which must be reduced by 2.5 percent from a 1990 baseline level. NOx combine with volatile organic compounds (VOC) and strong sunlight to form the blankets of urban smog that plague many big U.S. cities.
NYMEX said the complex model specifications include the same oxygenation and benzene requirements as the simple model gasoline.
But some industry sources note that strictly speaking, oxygen additives like MTBE (methyl tertiary butyl ether) are not required in complex model gasoline.

But they add however that refiners will likely continue to use them both because they are working in the battle against air pollution and have become a peripheral but indispensable element of the worldwide gasoline production infrastructure.
The VOC emissions performance standard is a minimum reduction of 13.1 percent from the 1990 baseline, NYMEX said.
Also, NYMEX said the EPA does not intend to enforce the new emissions standards until May 1, 1998.
The fuel's volatility, or Reid Vapor Pressure (RVP) levels from April 1 through September 15 will be changed to a maximum 9.0 pounds per square inch from 8.3.

An Exchange offiicial noted the more lenient RVP standard, which effectively allows use of a more evaporative fuel during the hot summer months, reflects other improvements that allowed regulators to grant refiners flexibility on RVP, which is said to be rather expensive for oil refiners to reduce.
Unburned fuel vapors which escape out of most cars, are considered to be VOCs, which combine with NOx emissions and sunlight to form smog, particularly on searing summer days.
The Exchange also said NYMEX gasoline options will be listed according to their established schedule.
